extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/aesthetics and readers studying humour theory or comic writing
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic philosophical exposition (Henri Bergson) setting out conditions, mechanisms, and social functions that make things laughable; useful for theorists, critics, and writers seeking principled criteria for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic confined to the human sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic does not exist outside what is strictly human; one laughs at animals or objects only insofar as one perceives in them some resemblance to human attitudes, shapes or uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: laughing at a hat because of its human-shaped caprice; one may laugh at an animal only when it exhibits a human posture or expression. This frames the domain in which one should look for comic elements (human behaviour, social forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indifference / momentary anesthesia of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce its full effect, the comic demands a momentary anesthesia or suspension of emotion — laughter appeals to intelligence rather than to the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the spectator is emotionally engaged (pity, deep feeling), the comic is blunted. Example: a drama becomes comic if the audience isolates the action from its emotional accompaniment. Practical implication: comic writing often asks readers/audience to adopt a detached, spectator stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/collective condition (laughter needs an echo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is essentially social: it normally occurs in a group and presumes complicity or shared intelligence among laughers; laughter reverberates and is intensified by an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many comic effects rely on shared customs/ideas and may not translate between social groups. The same scene may provoke laughter when surrounded by companions but not when reported to an outsider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic as a social corrective / utilitarian function
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter serves a social function: it punishes and discourages mechanical inelasticity or eccentricity, thus helping society maintain adaptability and sociability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson cautions this is not purely benevolent justice — laughter is a spontaneous mechanism that may err (hit innocents, spare guilty). Use: view comedic humiliation as social signalling and corrective, not merely amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation / 'something mechanical encrusted on the living'
rubrics_metrics.description: The basal laughable element is the perception of mechanical rigidity, automatism, or inelasticity imposed on what ought to be flexible, spontaneous and alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: a runner who falls because his muscles continue their motion like a machine; a person acting by habit rather than adapting to present circumstances. This formula recurs as a leitmotiv for analysing comic phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in situations: accidental external cause of mechanical action
rubrics_metrics.description: Situational comic often stems from an external circumstance (slip, practical joke) that exposes habit-driven or mechanical behaviour, producing an involuntary, laughable action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: slipping on the street, practical jokes that make habitual actions fail. Distinguish accidental situational comic (surface-level) from deeper comic embeddedness in character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in character: internalised rigidity and fixed ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When mechanical inelasticity becomes part of a person's habitual mental life — fixed ideas, absentmindedness, or systematic eccentricity — the comic becomes embedded in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the absent-minded, the over-romantic dreamer (Don Quixote), characters whose fixed passions become coherent sources of repeated comic mishaps. Comic characters are often unconscious of their comic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic characters are ignorant of themselves (unconsciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A key trait of comic persons is their lack of self-awareness: they are visible to others as ridiculous while remaining blind to their own ridiculousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because they do not perceive their defect, they do not correct it; this unawareness multiplies comic effects and explains why laughter can function as a humiliation/corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vice as a detachable, ready-made rigidity (comic vices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vices that appear as externally imposed, ready-made frames (rather than deep, tragic passions) simplify character and make it comic — they act like mechanical additions to the person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish comic vice (superficial, detachable, lends rigidity) from tragic vice (deeply incorporated). This explains why comedies often have titles like 'The Miser' rather than proper names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy and imitatability
rubrics_metrics.description: A deformity or comic physiognomy tends to be laughable if a normally built person could successfully imitate it; imitatability of the defect is a criterion for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bergson's test: how a primitive, direct visual impression reveals a rigidity or habit that can be mimicked. If a deformity suggests habitual posture/rigidity, it is more likely to be comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of naturalness of cause (the more 'natural' the cause seems, the funnier the effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the spectator can perceive the origin or genesis of a comic effect — when the cause seems natural and credible — the effect is more comic; newly arisen or visible development amplifies laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: absentmindedness traced to an obsession grows funnier as we see it develop; a staged escalation from habit to mishap increases comedic power. Practical: show the growth/origin of the comic trait rather than presenting it as arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneous illusion of life + distinct impression of mechanical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: An arrangement of acts/events is comic when it gives us, in a single combination, the illusion of life but also the distinct impression of a mechanical arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jack-in-the-box and toys; theatrical devices where characters seem alive yet move like automata. This paradoxical co-presence of life and mechanism is central to many comic scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal methods of light comedy: repetition, inversion, reciprocal interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Light comedy commonly employs three processes: repetition, inversion, and reciprocal interference of series (interlocking sequences producing comic effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are compositional devices for writers/performers: repetition (refrain, running gag), inversion (roles/actions reversed), reciprocal interference (two series of actions colliding). Bergson cites them as technical processes for producing comic situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in words: play upon ideas and sounds; abridged reasonings
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic verbal effects arise from shortened/defective reasonings, equivocations, puns, and eventually play upon sound rather than sense; these mimic dream-like or slackened logical tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: witticisms that give only the beginning and end of a reasoning; dialogues that degenerate into sound-play as meaning thins. Use: verbal comedy may shift from meaning to phonetic effects as relations between ideas become superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream-like logic, repetition and crescendo to absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Many comic scenes mirror dream processes: images recur across contexts, reasonings lose tension and accumulate absurd concessions culminating in an escalating absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Molière's plays that begin reasonably then drift into a dream-like succession of absurdities; Mark Twain dialogues that blend identities. Practically, gradual accumulation and repetition can intensify comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and social specificity of comic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Some comic effects are tied to the customs and ideas of particular social groups and may resist translation to other languages or cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for creators: check whether jokes depend on culturally specific knowledge; for critics: evaluate cross-cultural translatability as a dimension of a joke's universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic invites temporary relaxation (relief from intellectual tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic provides a release from the continuous effort of common sense and disciplined attention; it gives the spectator a brief, pleasurable suspension of work (playful, dolce far niente).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains the spectator's initial sympathy with comic characters and why comic scenes feel like a respite; however, relief is short-lived because laughter is also corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity and imprecision of laughter (not always just or kind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is a spontaneous, natural mechanism set up by social life; it hits without reflective deliberation and therefore may be unjust or unkind in particulars while aiming at a general corrective effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to temper normative claims about comedy's moral correctness: laughter's utility operates on averages, not perfect individual justice. Creators should be mindful of the potentially harsh social consequences of humiliation.
